data.title: Trump says he will create 'AI Force,' name AI czar
data.description:
Trump says he will create 'AI Force,' name AI czar

Reuters
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 5:35 pm UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON, Sept 19 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump ‌wrote in a social ‌media post on Saturday that ​he is creating an "AI Force" to oversee regulation of AI and will announce ‌an ⁠AI "czar" in the near future.

"We will not ⁠in any way hinder or stifle the Growth ​of this ​incredible ​Industry," Trump wrote ‌on Truth Social. "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows! However, ‌we will ​also be looking ​for ​BAD, and we ‌can do that, very ​easily, ​with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice ​System."

(Reporting ‌by Susan Heavey; Editing ​by Sergio Non and ​Rod Nickel)

data.title: Ex-Trump Comms Official Says President’s Media Ban Is A Sign He’s ‘Melting Down’
data.description:
Ex-Trump Comms Official Says President’s Media Ban Is A Sign He’s ‘Melting Down’

Pocharapon Neammanee
Updated Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:49 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump's former White House Press Secretary Stephanie Grisham tore into her old boss Friday night after he banned news outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House in a move she said "didn't surprise" her at all.

Grisham told CNN's Brianna Keilar that during his first term, Trump "tasked" her with "getting the press corps off the White House grounds."

"He had me looking at places that they could go that were off the White House grounds because he wanted everybody kicked out, not just the few that you guys are dealing with right now. I'm sure it'll get bigger," she said.

See Grisham's comments below:

Grisham said would "push it off and stall him" when Trump made the request, but she predicted he would pursue the goal again when he came back into power. 

"That's something that I knew was going to happen, watching him and the way he's just tearing down East Wings and doing whatever he wants," she said. "He clearly feels very, very empowered right now. So it didn't surprise me at all."

Politics: Melania Trump Shares 9-Second Glimpse Inside White House And… Yikes

The president announced his ban on Truth Social, accusing the three media outlets of being "FAKE NEWS!" 

"They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration," he said at a press conference Friday.

Grisham said she had hoped there would be someone in the White House telling him not to pursue the media ban.

"But it seems like he has really surrounded himself with sycophants and doesn't have the guardrails that we kind of had in Trump 1.0," she said.

"And so I think everybody's laughing and thinking it's a great idea, but you know, as always, he's missed it, the point," she said before railing against his administration's handling of the economy. 

"People don't care that the White House isn't, or that the press can't be on the White House grounds, because they're suffering, and he's not doing anything, but these silly projects and these silly little vanity, you know, issues that he's doing," Grisham continued. "And so once again, it's just not good. It doesn't look good. He's so out of touch, and he's melting down.

data.title: The September 11 cancer wave ahead
data.description:
The September 11 cancer wave ahead

Brenda Goodman, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:00 pm UTC
13 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

After the collapse came the dust. It billowed across Lower Manhattan in the wake of the 2001 World Trade Center terror attacks, turning people into ghosts as they trudged to safety.

It blew into buildings through broken windows and air intakes, settling into carpets, curtains and upholstery and leaving a fine powder on surfaces. People wrote messages in the dust coating the windows of buildings.

Despite official assurances at the time, the dust was toxic — loaded with finely pulverized building materials, as well as the byproducts of jet fuel combustion and vaporized heavy metals like cadmium, lead and mercury.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that as many as 400,000 people were exposed. Some were first responders like firefighters and paramedics, but others were put in harm's way because they returned to contaminated apartments, schools and offices in Lower Manhattan or Brooklyn, where they breathed in contaminants.

As a result, more people have now died of environmental illnesses that followed the September 11 attacks than perished during the collapse of the towers that day.

Over the past 25 years, the mix of problems experienced by September 11 survivors has changed, too. About half of the 54,000 survivors who have qualified for financial help through the World Trade Center Health Program now have cancer, roughly triple the number who had the same diagnosis five years ago, according to CDC data.

The likelihood that a person will get cancer increases with age, so it's not surprising that people who lived through the World Trade Center attacks would be more likely to get cancer 25 years later. But there are signs that some of these cancers are linked to the toxic dust people were breathing for months after the attacks, and aren't just a factor of aging. Rare "sentinel cancers" such as mesothelioma are beginning to show up in World Trade Center survivors, and they appear to be more prevalent than in the general population.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"This is one of the largest man-made disasters in the history of United States," said Dr. Alan Arslan, a cancer epidemiologist at NYU Langone Medical Center who studies September 11 survivors. "And it is also a disaster characterized by a very complex exposure to many, many potential carcinogens, including asbestos."

Dr. Leigh Wilson, who directs the World Trade Center Environmental Center — one of seven clinical centers of excellence in the New York area that treat people exposed after the World Trade Center disaster — and works with Arslan, said their program continues to receive about 120 new patients each month.

Enrollment is picking up as people realize they qualify for care. When the program was launched in 2012, more first responders signed up than "survivors": people who lived, worked or went to school within a certain area around ground zero. But over time, the number of new survivor enrollments each year has outpaced those of first responders. Roughly twice as many survivors as first responders enrolled in the program in 2024 and 2025, according to CDC data.

"I think it's very well understood that [first] responders are eligible for the World Trade Center Health Program, but a lot of survivors don't realize that they are eligible," Wilson said.

A rare and deadly cancer increases in 9/11 survivors

One of the chief concerns in the wake of the tragedy was the hundreds of tons of asbestos that had been used as a fireproofing material in one of the towers and blasted free in the attacks.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Asbestos has tiny needle-like fibers that burrow deep into tissue, creating chronic inflammation that spurs the development of cancers of the lungs, voice box and ovaries. It also causes a rare and aggressive cancer called mesothelioma, or cancer of the mesothelium, the thin layer of tissue that protects internal organs like the lungs and abdomen.

Mesothelioma is what's known as a sentinel cancer. Almost always, when doctors diagnose it, they also know exactly how how it happened: through exposure to asbestos. Very few cancers have ever been so closely linked to an environmental agent.

Still, exposure doesn't guarantee a person will get mesothelioma. Somewhere between 1 in 8 and 1 in 13 people who are heavily exposed to asbestos on the job will develop the cancer later in life. And mesothelioma isn't the only way asbestos makes people sick; it can also cause lung cancer and progressive scarring of the lungs called asbestosis.

But mesothelioma does offer cancer researchers one of the clearest pictures they have of cause and effect. Many chemical exposures, for example, have been linked to breast and prostate cancers, cancers that are also prevalent in World Trade Center survivors, but so are lifestyle factors and genes, making it a thorny problem to tease out the cause of any one person's cancer after an environmental disaster. Not so with mesothelioma.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Because of this, researchers see it as a kind of harbinger.

"Rates are only going to go up," said Dr. Jacqueline Moline, who directs the World Trade Center Health Program at Northwell Health. "This will be a foreshadowing" of the cancer burden ahead.

Moline says 38 cases of mesothelioma have been diagnosed among the nearly 155,000 people enrolled in the World Trade Center Health Program to date, an incidence that already appears to be about three times as high as in the general population.

And it's still early. Mesothelioma takes its time to show up, said Dr. Raja Flores, chairman of the department of thoracic surgery at Mount Sinai Health System, who has pioneered treatments for the disease.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I think what we're seeing now is actually the beginning. The latency period for mesothelioma can be 25 to 50 years," he said. It's not the most common cancer showing up after the World Trade Center attacks, but "mesothelioma is a very important one because it's practically a death sentence for most people."

How ordinary people were exposed

For one of the residents enrolled in the survivor group, a man who was 23 at the time of the attacks, it took 15 years.

The man lived a few blocks from the World Trade Center. He told investigators he was exposed to the large dust cloud on September 11. He left his apartment for a week after the attacks, and he came home to a light coating of dust on its surfaces. He cleaned up the dust but never had his space professionally cleaned.

He remembered World Trade Center dust being present in his apartment for more than a month after the attacks. He saw it in the air every day for months.

Aside from living close to the Twin Towers, the man appeared to have no other risk factors. He didn't smoke and wasn't overweight.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In 2012, the man began to have abdominal pain and bloating. Four years later, when doctors performed a minimally invasive procedure to repair what they suspected was a hernia, they found something else.

He was diagnosed in 2016, at age 38, with mesothelioma of his abdominal wall. He had aggressive surgery to cut out the tumors and "hot wash" chemotherapy, in which doctors filled his abdominal cavity with warmed cancer-killing medications to destroy any microscopic tumors that remained.

His case was among four described in a study of mesothelioma in World Trade Center survivors in 2024. He responded well to the treatment and was still alive when the report was published. Two of the four patients had died of their cancers, however.

In a December 2001 memo included among the newly released documents, Cate Jenkins, an environmental scientist in the Waste Identification Branch at the US Environmental Protection Agency, did some rough calculations of the risk people might face from living or working near the Twin Towers after September 11.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In a scenario eerily like the actual case described by the World Trade Center Health Program, Jenkins calculated the increased risk to a person who was enveloped by the initial dust cloud walking back to their apartment in Lower Manhattan and who left for a few days after but came back and tried to clean their own apartment.

In that case, she wrote, the increased risk of getting mesothelioma would be 1 in 100, about 100 times above the EPA's acceptable threshold for cancer risk from an environmental exposure. If the person continued to live in that apartment for the next 15 years, their risk for mesothelioma would rise to 1 in 10, which is 1,000 times above the EPA's threshold.

New documents highlight flawed testing and communication

Jenkins' memo was part of a cache of new documents made public last week by New York City officials in response to two Freedom of Information Act lawsuits filed by the 9/11 Health Watch advocacy group.

Even as internal discussions were sounding the alarm, health officials were making reassuring statements to the public.

In a statement issued a week after the attacks, EPA Administrator Christine Whitman said that air testing in New York and Washington showed that people in those areas were not being exposed to "excessive levels of asbestos or other harmful substances."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Given the scope of the tragedy last week, I am glad to reassure the people of New York and Washington DC that their air is safe to breathe, and their water is safe to drink," Whitman was said a news release. It was only one of many repeated assurances to people who were living or working near the site.

Fifteen years later, Whitman apologized in media interviews. "I'm very sorry that people are sick," she told the Guardian. "I'm very sorry that people are dying, and if the EPA and I in any way contributed to that, I'm sorry. We did the very best we could at the time with the knowledge we had."

Investigations later showed that these statements were based on flawed testing.

Early on, the EPA was primarily focused on asbestos levels in outdoor air and didn't test inside many buildings, where pollutants can concentrate and become trapped, resulting in higher exposures.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The agency also relied on testing thresholds for asbestos that were not health-based.

"Asbestos is unsafe at any amount," said Kimberly Flynn, director of the nonprofit advocacy group 9/11 Environmental Action.

"The EPA said it was safe many, many, many times and said that that declaration of safety was based on science, which it was not," said Flynn, who is herself a World Trade Center survivor.

As a result, Flynn said, many people simply didn't realize the danger they were in and didn't take steps they should have to protect themselves.

Additionally, the agency's tests relied on a less sensitive optical microscopy method that can see only larger asbestos fibers. The intensity of the World Trade Center collapse created a range of sizes of asbestos fibers, including some that were very small, which were later picked up by a more sensitive technology: transmission electron microscopy.

This testing, which was commissioned by the Ground Zero Elected Officials Task Force, a group started by Rep. Jarrold Nadler, found that levels of asbestos in two apartment buildings near the World Trade Center were "significantly elevated."

Jenkins, the EPA environmental scientist, later said the scientists, who were asbestos testing experts and EPA contractors, found nine asbestos fibers for every one found by the EPA.

Their report recommended that indoor spaces be cleaned by professionals with experience removing asbestos and that residents not reoccupy those spaces until after they had been cleared.

Instead, New York officials recommended that people clean their own apartments with wet mops and wet rags and if possible with vacuum cleaners with HEPA filters.

Many of these homes were not cleaned using even these minimally protective methods, however, according to a door-to-door survey conducted shortly after the attacks by the New York City Department of Health.

"People went home to poison, while the government that was supposed to protect them looked the other way," said Linda Reinstein, president and co-founder of the nonprofit Asbestos Disease Awareness Association.

As a result, environmental health specialists believe, residents were probably re-exposed to the toxins in the dust in their own homes for months after the attacks. Anything that could stir up the dust – such as vacuuming the carpet, sweeping the floor, even just tracking it in on their shoes – could stir up the dust again.

"The composition of the World Trade Center material should also have demanded caution," said Dr. Richard Peltier, a professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts at Amherst.

"This was not ordinary urban particulate matter. The collapse pulverized concrete, gypsum wallboard, glass fibers, carpeting, stored chemicals and other building materials. The fires and destruction added metals, asbestos and a complex mixture of combustion products and organic chemicals. In effect, thousands of tons of materials that were never intended to be inhaled were crushed, burned, aerosolized and deposited across a densely populated urban area.

"I think this changes how we should think about September 11. The mortality from the World Trade Center disaster did not end when the buildings fell. The health consequences have continued to accumulate for 25 years."

data.title: Teen’s key role in deadly San Diego mosque shooting leads to murder charges in North Carolina, officials say. Here’s why
data.description:
Teen’s key role in deadly San Diego mosque shooting leads to murder charges in North Carolina, officials say. Here’s why

Julianna Bragg, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:00 pm UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

A teen in North Carolina who prosecutors say played a key role in the deadly San Diego mosque shooting — by livestreaming the attack and disseminating the shooters' writings — is facing murder charges in her home state.

Under North Carolina's aiding-and-abetting laws, which can hold someone criminally responsible for a crime even if they did not personally carry out the acts, 17-year-old Sarah Santiago faces three counts of first-degree murder and one count of conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.

Prosecutors say Santiago can be held responsible for the three killings because she assisted the shooters in carrying out the attack from behind the scenes, despite not being at the Islamic Center of San Diego, the site of the attacks.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The law in North Carolina is clear: A person may be guilty of a crime, although he or she personally does not do any of the acts necessary to constitute the crime," Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O'Neill said in August.

Authorities say on May 18, Cain Clark, 17, and Caleb Vazquez, 18, opened fire on San Diego's largest mosque, killing beloved community members Amin Abdullah, Mansour Kaziha and Nadir Awad — hailed as heroes for their actions thwarting further killings — before the gunmen died by suicide, according to law enforcement.

Santiago is accused of aiding and abetting the murders of the three men by "agreeing and planning prior to the attack" to livestream it, publicly distributing the recording and releasing a manifesto "purporting to justify the attack," the indictment alleges.

Santiago has not entered a plea, her attorney Alan Doorasamy said Friday. Last month, he told CNN in an email that "at this time I can confirm that my client is innocent of all these charges."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Ronald Wright, a criminal law professor at Wake Forest University, described the circumstances of Santiago's case as highly "unusual" for North Carolina, as she faces prosecution on the opposite side of the country from California.

San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan told CNN that North Carolina was given priority to lead the prosecution because, unlike California law — which requires a judge to hold a "transfer hearing" to consider moving the case from youth to adult court — North Carolina law allows for a juvenile to be initially charged and prosecuted as an adult in certain circumstances, such as murder charges.

Santiago's next hearing is scheduled for September 21, the first of what could be a lengthy series of court proceedings as the case moves forward.

Her attorney, Doorasamy, told CNN that, as of Thursday, the state had not provided him with discovery, adding he will file motions to compel discovery by September 21 if necessary.

Gunmen's writings contained radicalized ideology

Before the attacks, prosecutors say Santiago bought and sent Vazquez a Sonnenrad patch, which the indictment alleges he wore during the shooting. A Sonnenrad is viewed as a neo-Nazi and white supremacist hate symbol.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Authorities believe the shooters "exchanged radicalized ideology," some of which was in the "manifesto" police found that covered "a wide aspect of races and religions." Hate speech was also found scrawled on one of the weapons used in the attack, and a suicide note contained writings about racial pride, officials said.

More than 30 guns, including numerous pistols, rifles and shotguns, a crossbow, tactical gear, ammunition and electronics, were found by authorities while executing three search warrants at residences associated with the attackers.

Clark's mother called police officers after she found an alleged suicide note written by her son, who vanished with a man he met online she had never seen before — both dressed in camouflage, according to San Diego Police Chief Scott Wahl. She also reported several weapons from the home were missing, the police chief said.

Vazquez had been in a mental health program up until the day before the shooting, a federal law enforcement official told CNN.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

On the morning of the shooting, Vazquez's mother received a call from employees at the facility, who said her son was missing, according to The Associated Press. Video footage recorded Vazquez as he left the facility at 8 p.m. the night before.

Law enforcement also filed a gun violence emergency protective order in 2025, after Vazquez was placed on a psychiatric hold, to seize firearms in his parents' home amid concerns about the teenager's "suspicious behavior idolizing Nazis and mass shooters," court documents show.

Following the mosque attack, the shooters planned to commit mass murder at a Jewish temple and target African American students at a public high school, authorities said. But the attackers may have stopped because one of them was wounded by an armed security officer at the mosque, federal law enforcement officials told CNN.

What happens next?

Monday's hearing is expected to be preliminary in nature, Wright said, though it's unlikely that a significant amount of new information will be revealed, given that officials have already released the indictment and made previous statements.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Wright said some of the central questions for the jury would include whether prosecutors proved beyond a reasonable doubt that Santiago's actions aided and abetted the killings and that she intended to cause the death of another human being.

Under North Carolina's aiding-and-abetting theory, prosecutors will need to prove not only that Santiago "knowingly advised, instigated, encouraged, procured, or aided the other person to commit" the murders, but also that her "actions or statements caused or contributed to the commission" of the murders by the shooters, the law says.

"If the jury believes she did something that helped and she had a purpose to cause the death of another human being through her friends who were going to pull the trigger, then that would be enough" to prove her guilt, he said.

Santiago's defense is expected to challenge the prosecution's arguments, including the question of whether North Carolina courts have jurisdiction over someone who allegedly helped with a crime but did not carry out any of the physical acts in California, Wright said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

In California, which also has a similar aiding-and-abetting law, prosecutors could also pursue charges against Santiago, Wright said, though it remains unclear whether they will do so while the North Carolina case proceeds.

Given the high visibility of the murder case, it could take months or even years for Santiago's case to play out in state court, Wright said.

As Santiago's case proceeds, officials in both states say they intend to continue pursuing potential avenues of accountability for those involved in the attack.

"We are keeping the families of these heroes up to date as to what is happening on all fronts," Stephan said. "The San Diego District Attorney's Office will not stop investigating this matter until all those who can be held liable for their actions are."

CNN's Dianne Gallagher contributed to this report.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

data.title: ‘It will never be the same’: How Trump turned on the Kennedy Center and brought it to its knees
data.description:
‘It will never be the same’: How Trump turned on the Kennedy Center and brought it to its knees

Jeremy Herb, Sunlen Serfaty, Jacqui Palumbo, CNN
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 4:00 pm UTC
11 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

When President Donald Trump's name was ordered removed from the Kennedy Center this spring, it seemed that an opening to move on from his reign over the performing arts center might have emerged.

"I have instructed the Department of Commerce to make all necessary arrangements with Congress to allow a full and complete transfer of this Institution, giving them the responsibility for its Operation, Maintenance, and Management," the president wrote in a late-May Truth Social post, seemingly relinquishing the control he'd seized a year prior.

Speculation even bubbled up among some of the more than a dozen "ex-officio," board members — who don't get a vote but are not allied with Trump — over whether the former board chairman, billionaire philanthropist David Rubenstein, could be brought back to help restore the center's fundraising and programming, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN. (CNN has asked Rubenstein for comment.)

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But after Trump said he would remain chairman, "it kind of all squelched pretty quickly," one of the sources said. The hope that his crusade to rename a monument dedicated to the memory of John F. Kennedy had ended turned out to be wishful thinking.

Instead, nine months from a cold December day when cranes first placed Trump's name on the marble façade, the institution has been brought to the brink by the president still very much engaged in a fight: lights have been turned off inside, infrastructure is crumbling and protests swirl while legal battles mount.

A lawsuit brought by Democratic Rep. Joyce Beatty of Ohio, an ex-officio board member, led to a judge's ruling that Trump's name had to be scraped off the building and that the board could not shut down the facility altogether.

Trump has only ratcheted up his threats to tear down the building in response to the legal setbacks: The president was seen with a poster this week through the window of Air Force One that appeared to read "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED." Though the federal judge has since ordered a 30-day notice be given before any major change happens, it's not at all clear where things go from here.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Late Friday night, the administration argued in court that the Kennedy Center must close for two years, asking the federal judge in the case to allow it so that the "dangerously dilapidated and decrepit" building can be renovated.

On the same day, over a dozen Kennedy Center employees were laid off, including its lead spokesperson, according to two sources familiar with the matter — gutting an already skeleton staff. The Kennedy Center declined to comment on the cuts.

Trump has said previous leadership is to blame for the dire financial situation. During a contentious board call this week, he also blamed Beatty for bringing litigation that, he said, has contributed to the center's downfall.

While the president and his allies on the board argue his name needs to be re-affixed to the building to revive fundraising, current and former officials, performers and industry officials say it is precisely Trump's involvement that alienated the center's donors and prompted scores of artists to cancel their performances.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The Broadway productions will not come back, the artists will not come back," said a source familiar with discussions about programming. "None of those donors will come back as long as Donald J Trump is the chairman."

Current and former Kennedy Center officials, musicians, artists and other performers with ties to the center suggest that Trump's takeover has added a permanent imprint on the Kennedy Center, whether or not his name ultimately ends up on the building.

"There are wonderful theaters throughout this country, and they are certainly part of the cultural ecology," said LaRue Allen, president and executive director of the Martha Graham Dance Company, which has a 50-year history with the institution. "But the Kennedy Center — it is our nation's capital. It is our national showcase."

Another Kennedy Center source who recently left said simply: "It will never be the same."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

CNN has asked the White House for comment.

'The Kennedy Center, they do a beautiful job, an incredible job'

Trump's focus on the Kennedy Center is emblematic of a notable shift from his first administration to a second one that has targeted arts, cultural and educational pillars across the country, in addition to Trump's unrelenting desire to remake the nation's capital to his liking.

In his first term, Trump mostly avoided the venue, skipping the Kennedy Center Honors after awardees threatened to boycott the event if he attended. The White House even said in a 2017 statement that the president and First Lady Melania Trump were not participating "to allow the honorees to celebrate without any political distraction."

And when the Kennedy Center initially received $25 million in funding in a March 2020 Covid stimulus package, Trump defended the aid, saying: "The Kennedy Center, they do a beautiful job, an incredible job."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Nine months later, however, he singled out a $40 million line-item for the center while criticizing a subsequent December 2020 Covid aid bill — a foreshadowing of his future disaffection.

By his 2024 campaign, Trump made clear that going after so-called "wokeism" would be a pillar of a second presidency. He didn't appear to single out the Kennedy Center on the campaign trail, but in his third week in office he'd already set a takeover plan in motion.

"At my direction, we are going to make the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C., GREAT AGAIN," Trump wrote on Truth Social in February 2025.

Trump said he had fired Rubenstein as chairman of the board as well as board trustees "who do not share our Vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The takeover became the first domino in a cascade of Trump moves to remake the nation's capital, including the demolition of the East Wing of the White House, the closure and remodeling of the busiest public golf course in Washington, DC, and his ongoing efforts to build a 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery — projects all still being fought over in court.

Though Trump has widely criticized cultural institutions and museums, he's been able to exert only so much control over them, primarily by reducing their federal funding. The federal government has gutted the agencies that fund the arts, including the National Endowment for the Arts and National Endowment for the Humanities, and denied and rescinded tens of millions of dollars in grants to organizations that don't align with the president's values.

But the Kennedy Center is one of the few cultural institutions where the president has been able to flex more of his power by seizing control of the board. He has similarly tried to bring the federally funded Smithsonian Institution to heel, with more uneven results.

A week after Trump's board takeover, the president was named as its chairman, and he installed longtime loyalist Richard Grenell as executive director.

"So we took over the Kennedy Center," Trump told reporters. "I'm going to be chairman of it, and we're going to make sure that it's good and it's not going to be woke. There's no more woke in this country."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

His new role prompted several cancellations, including most notably the Broadway show "Hamilton."

Leading up to the center's Kennedy Center Honors in December 2025, which Trump himself was hosting, the president began referring to the building as the "Trump Kennedy Center."

On December 18, 2025, the board made that declaration official by voting to rename the facility the "The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts," saying that the change honored Trump's work at the center after taking over.

One day later, new signage was installed to add Trump's name to the building's façade.

A legal and financial saga

The legal battle and wave of cancellations that has ensued present particular challenges for an institution that makes part of its budget from ticket sales.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Operating as a non-profit, the Kennedy Center received roughly $37 million from Congress in the last fiscal year, according to the latest appropriations legislation signed into law. But the bulk of its revenue comes from programming and private donations. In fiscal year 2024, during the Biden administration, the Kennedy Center reported $307 million in revenues, according to documents filed with the IRS.

Last year, Grenell sought to revamp the center's calendar to include, in his words, more family-friendly programming. He brought in "Dog Man: The Musical," based on the popular kids' graphic novel series, at the recommendation of second lady Usha Vance.

At the same time, the center became a place to host events that lean in to Trumpian ties, including the premiere of the documentary "Melania," a Charlie Kirk memorial and the FIFA World Cup draw (where the organization gave Trump a peace prize).

But after Trump's name was added to the building, a wave of performers pulled out, and ticket sales sagged. Multiple sources told CNN earlier this year that attendance at the Kennedy Center had been so low that for months it had to "paper the house" — a theater term that means to fill seats by offering free or discounted tickets.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"There was a haze of despair around the performances. Nobody was showing up to performances," Carlos Simon, the Kennedy Center composer-in-residence since 2021, told CNN.

Simon, who is in the last year of his residence, noted that the National Symphony Orchestra is now playing at other venues in Washington. He said he's stayed in his role at the Kennedy Center "for the morale of the folks who were still there trying to do the good work of presenting music."

"I feel really bad that it's become this political tool or pawn, but music still has to go on," he said.

Amid the cancellations, Trump announced in February that the Kennedy Center would close for two years on July 4 to allow for renovations — a move critics suspected was to being made more to provide cover for the shrinking pool of patrons than because of the need for such a dramatic closure.

The Kennedy Center also received an influx of funding last year thanks to Trump's "One Big Beautiful Bill," which contained $257 million for the center to pursue "necessary expenses for capital repair, restoration, maintenance backlog, and security structures."

Yet the board has argued only Trump's help can muster the funds to renovate the building — and Trump has made clear his help will only come with naming rights.

In the meantime, Matt Floca, Grenell's successor as executive director, this week told the judge in the Beatty case that the center needs to temporarily close due to safety concerns.

Even if the building survives, officials say getting the center's programming to return — particularly Broadway shows — would still take months if not several years.

That is under the assumption, of course, that performances would be willing to return, said the source involved in the center's programming.

"If we started now in terms of engaging with property companies, going back and forth and getting a deal made, we could have Broadway tours back at the Kennedy Center by the basically middle of '27 into '28," the source said. "That's how long it takes for all these pieces to be put in place."

CNN's Katelyn Polantz contributed to this report.

Sept 19 (Reuters) - The White House on Saturday denied access to journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, following through with US President Donald Trump's announcement that ‌he would ban them from the building's grounds.

All three news outlets separately said their teams' ‌press passes were confiscated on Saturday morning when their journalists went to the White House. They have signaled that they may contest the ​ban on the grounds that it conflicts with the US Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press.

A CNN statement on Saturday called the ban "an illegal assault" on its constitutional right to do journalism without interference from the government. In separate statements, MS NOW and Politico said they would "defend our First ‌Amendment rights".

MS NOW said it intends ⁠to "take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy."

CNN and MS NOW said they ⁠would continue reporting on the Trump administration, and Politico said it stands by its reporters covering the White House.

A social media post by Trump on Friday accused the outlets of "reporting FAKE NEWS" and said that they "shouldn't ​be able ​to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES ​when they're covering the President of the ‌United States."

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, Trump answered a question about what he meant by other outlets by describing the New York Times and the Washington Post as examples of "fake news," although he did not specifically say he would ban them from the White House.

The New York Times in a statement called Trump's latest ban "yet another retaliatory ‌and unconstitutional threat" and said the newspaper "stands in support of ​the news organizations being unfairly targeted by the president."

data.title: Greenland, Denmark say Trump deal won't compromise sovereignty
data.description:
Greenland, Denmark say Trump deal won't compromise sovereignty

By Stine Jacobsen, Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen and Tom Little
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 3:47 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Special Report: How Trump's threats to seize Greenland have upended the island's push for independence

1 of 2
A drone view shows houses on the shore of Nuuk, Greenland, February 7, 2026. REUTERS/Stoyan Nenov

By Stine Jacobsen, Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen and Tom Little

COPENHAGEN, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Denmark and Greenland on Saturday said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland's sovereignty, after President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington "permanent control" over the Arctic ‌island's security, leaving its precise scope unclear.

The United States, Denmark and Greenland said late on Friday they had reached an agreement ‌for the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Key details of the agreement have not been made ​public, including the scale of US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.

Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump's threats to seize control of Greenland.

"Next week could be a good week - for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States," Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke ‌Rasmussen said in a statement posted on Facebook ⁠on Saturday.

"A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe - while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom's red lines," he ⁠said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But some residents in Greenland's capital Nuuk expressed scepticism about closer ties with Washington.

"The US should not control Greenland. I think it's better if we have cooperation with NATO," said Jakob Ludvigsen, 65.

"Trump should stay far, far, far away from Greenland," Marianne Hansen, a 71-year-old retired chef, told Reuters in Nuuk. "He should not expect our ​children ​and grandchildren to become Americans in the future."

Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly insisted that ​Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and ‌accept that Greenland is not for sale.

TRUMP'S VISION FOR GREENLAND DEAL

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump said on Truth Social on Friday that under a deal, "the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America."

The deal "gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Trump said, adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington's express written approval.

Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively ‌reported that the US and Denmark were closing in on a deal.

"This is probably ​not the end of President Trump's ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of ​US strategic interest in the territory and its resources," said Mikkel Vedby ​Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

If Copenhagen cedes any formal authority to Washington, it raises ‌the question in Greenland of whether "this is the beginning of ​replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with ​a colonial relationship to the United States," he said.

Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a Facebook post on Saturday that the proposed deal "recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination."

Trump's threats, which peaked in January, ​triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations within NATO ‌and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.

A NATO spokesperson on Saturday said the alliance welcomed the agreement, ​which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region."

(Reporting by Stine Jacobsen and Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen, Additional reporting by ​Tim Barsoe in Nuuk and Lili Bayer in Brussels; Editing by Ros Russell)

German general Breuer elected to head top NATO military body

Reuters

2 min read

BRUSSELS, Sept 19 (Reuters) - General Carsten Breuer, Germany's chief of defence, was chosen on Saturday as the next head of NATO's military committee, the ‌alliance's top military authority and a key advisory body for its political leaders.

Military ‌chiefs from the 32-nation alliance elected Breuer at a meeting in Copenhagen, current chair Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo ​Dragone said in a post on X. Breuer will take up the role next summer, succeeding Dragone.

"Your operational judgement, your deep familiarity with this Alliance and your leadership of the German Armed Forces will serve NATO well," Dragone wrote, congratulating Breuer.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The Chiefs of Defence have ‌placed their trust in you ⁠at a demanding moment for Euro-Atlantic security," he added.

The committee is NATO's senior military authority and its chair serves as the main ⁠military adviser to its political chief, Secretary General Mark Rutte.

Breuer will assume the post at a time of upheaval in the alliance. US President Donald Trump has demanded that European countries ​take ​primary responsibility for the continent's defence after decades ​of American leadership.

Many European governments have ‌ramped up defence spending in recent years, driven both by Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and by Trump's threats not to honour US commitments to NATO.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Germany, Europe's largest economy, has been at the forefront of the spending surge. Berlin aims to double its military expenditure to over €200 billion ($230 billion) by 2030.

Breuer, a 61-year-old army officer, earned the ‌nickname "the chancellor's general" after then-Chancellor Olaf Scholz picked ​him to lead a crisis committee that helped manage ​Germany's response to the COVID pandemic in ​2021 and 2022.

He joined the Bundeswehr in an air defence unit ‌in 1984 and later attended the ​US general staff college ​in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, as well as German general staff training in Hamburg. In 2014, he served with NATO's International Security Assistance Force in the Afghan ​capital Kabul.

Germany's current army chief, ‌Lieutenant General Christian Freuding, is expected to succeed Breuer as chief of ​defence before the end of the year.

data.title: Denmark hails 'binding' Greenland deal with Trump
data.description:
Denmark hails 'binding' Greenland deal with Trump

Camille BAS-WOHLERT
Sat, 19 September 2026 at 3:30 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Denmark on Saturday hailed a "binding" deal announced by US President Donald Trump to give Washington "permanent control" over Greenland's security and bar Russian and Chinese bases from the Arctic territory.

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.

Denmark and Greenland -- an autonomous Danish territory -- both hailed the agreement and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"A long period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and North Atlantic," Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said in a social media post on Saturday.

The deal respected Denmark's "red lines" and was "important" in light of a changed security situation, he said.

- 'Permanent control' -

While the terms are still unclear, Denmark maintains that its sovereignty remains intact.

Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the agreement with Washington "recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination".

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It was "good for NATO and Europe", she said.

Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal "recognises Greenland's interests" and "strengthens" its security.

Trump hailed it as an "'Infinite Life' Agreement, there is no end!". Washington would immediately start building up a large military presence in the territory, he added.

"From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."

While Trump presented the deal as a major triumph, Danish commentators said he had likely gained little.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

They noted that, under a 1951 defence pact updated in 2004, Washington was already able to ramp up its military presence on the island provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance.

"Shhh. Don't tell Trump that it's the Kingdom of Denmark that has prevailed," US correspondent Jacob Heinel Jensen wrote in Danish newspaper Berlingske on Saturday.

Ulrik Pram Gad, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, said Trump "obviously didn't get in this agreement what he originally set out to have, that is, sovereign control over all of Greenland as a part of the United States".

- Details unclear -

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump has repeatedly warned of Russia and China trying to establish a foothold in Greenland as a strategic battle unfolds for supremacy in a warming Arctic. The State Department left no doubt that they would not be allowed to do so.

"This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors," a State Department official said.

Gad noted that while Russia had little interest in Greenland, China was investing in extractive industries to get a foothold in the Arctic.

"The US is worried that any kind of Chinese footprint could be turned into military assets," he said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Cautioning that the details of the deal were still unknown, Gad said "the worrisome thing here is this exclusive access for the US to build bases in Greenland and how that involves NATO allies from Europe.

"Trump has been flirting with breaking up the NATO alliance... If Europe is an adversary, how would that position Europe, Denmark and Greenland in that situation?" he said.

Furthermore, "if the US can also veto European investments in Greenland, that would be highly controversial."

- NATO tensions -

Trump gave no details about the deal, but several media outlets have reported that the United States wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and NATO.

Tensions have since eased, and in an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.

Danes strolling in Copenhagen on Saturday were cautiously optimistic.

"I hope this is a definitive and sound deal once the details are known but I wouldn't be surprised if we have to take a step back again and then hopefully two steps forward," Soren, a 52-year-old IT executive, told AFP.
